chunks: "The standard is FR-4, woven glass in epoxy: cheap, stiff, easy to process, with a dielectric constant around 4. 2 to 4. 7 and a loss tangent around 0. 02.
It's the right choice up to a gigahertz or so and for most products.

Its trade-offs are loss at high frequency, a dielectric constant that varies with frequency and with the glass weave, a glass transition around 130 to 180 degrees Celsius, and poor thermal conductivity, about 0.
3 watts/mK. For more demanding cases you move to other materials. High-Tg FR-4 survives lead-free assembly better.
Polyimide, with a Tg above 250 degrees, is used for flex and high-temperature boards, at higher cost and with more moisture uptake.
For RF and microwave you use PTFE or ceramic-filled hydrocarbon laminates with a loss tangent of 0. 001 to 0.
004, stable permittivity, and much lower attenuation, but they cost several times more and are harder to process.
Ceramics like alumina and aluminium nitride handle high temperature and conduct heat much better, but are brittle and expensive.
And metal-core boards use a thin filled-epoxy dielectric on an aluminium base to get heat out of LEDs and power parts.
So the choice trades electrical performance, temperature, thermal conduction and cost, and I'd use FR-4 unless a requirement forces something else."
